patient.name: Niamh Gallagher
patient.setting: Hepatology clinic, after an urgent GP referral
patient.complaint: Six weeks of tiredness, aching joints and now yellow eyes
background: Drinks 4 units a week; no IV drug use; no recent travel

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a young woman who has another autoimmune disease, a hepatitic (ALT-dominant) LFT picture and often a raised IgG or ASMA in the stem.

points: Niamh, 27, has felt **exhausted** for six weeks.
Poor appetite, dull ache under her right ribs.
Knees and wrists ache; this week her **eyes turned yellow**.

steps.lead: Niamh's liver is being attacked by her own immune system: a **chronic** inflammatory process that, left alone, scars towards cirrhosis.
Young, **female** and already carrying two autoimmune diseases, with a mother who has Graves': Niamh is the textbook risk profile.

visual.title: Where Niamh's discomfort is
visual.caption: RUQ ache from a swollen, inflamed liver capsule; the liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.

points: No spider naevi, no ascites, no flap.
No rash; joints ache but are not swollen.

steps.lead: Fatigue, anorexia, RUQ pain, **arthralgia**, jaundice and hepatomegaly: an **acute-hepatitis-like** illness in a young woman.

steps.q: Niamh's LFTs show ALT 640 IU/L and ALP 160 IU/L. Which pattern is this?
steps.r: ALT up about 13-fold with ALP barely raised is a **hepatitic** (ALT-dominant) pattern, exactly what AIH gives.

steps.lead: Niamh's personal and family autoimmune history plus hepatitic LFTs point to **type 1** AIH; her antibodies will confirm it.

steps.title: Young woman with deranged LFTs: which liver disease?
head: Feature
Autoimmune hepatitis
Primary biliary cholangitis
Primary sclerosing cholangitis

steps.text: Do not pick viral hepatitis just because the LFTs are hepatitic. A young woman with **other autoimmune disease** and high IgG is AIH until proven otherwise.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (liver biopsy) or 'Which is the most likely finding?' (ASMA, anti-LKM or raised IgG).

steps.title: Niamh's first bloods
steps.text: Transaminases far higher than ALP, and a markedly raised **IgG**.

steps.lead: Niamh's **ALT-dominant** LFTs and high IgG fit; next comes the autoantibody screen, viral serology to exclude infection, and a liver ultrasound.

visual.title: Niamh's ALT against normal
visual.label: Niamh 640
visual.caption: Over 10 times the upper limit, with ALP only mildly raised.

steps.title: Autoantibody and viral screen
rows: HBsAg / anti-HCV / HAV IgM / HEV IgM
steps.text: ASMA and ANA positive, anti-LKM negative: **type 1** AIH. Viral causes excluded.

steps.q: Which result would point to type 2 rather than type 1 AIH?
steps.r: **Anti-LKM** defines type 2. ASMA (with ANA) is type 1; AMA is PBC; p-ANCA is PSC.

points: Liver ultrasound: smooth enlarged liver, normal bile ducts.
No gallstones, no focal lesion, patent portal vein.

steps.lead: Antibodies and IgG make AIH likely, but Niamh still needs a **liver biopsy**: the definitive, gold-standard test, read alongside the autoantibodies.

steps.text: Biopsy in AIH shows **interface hepatitis** with a lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate. In the exam, 'definitive' or 'gold standard' for AIH = **liver biopsy**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (prednisolone) or 'Which test must be done before starting azathioprine?' (TPMT activity).

steps.q: Biopsy confirms interface hepatitis. What is Niamh's first-line treatment?
steps.r: AIH is treated with **immunosuppression**, starting with **prednisolone**. Ursodeoxycholic acid is for PBC.

steps.lead: Niamh starts **prednisolone** to switch off the immune attack. She has type 1 diabetes, so her glucose needs closer monitoring on steroids.
To spare steroids, **azathioprine** is added, but only after Niamh's **TPMT activity** is checked to avoid pancytopenia.

steps.title: Before azathioprine
steps.text: Normal TPMT and a normal baseline count: standard-dose azathioprine is safe.

visual.title: Niamh's response to treatment
visual.caption: ALT and IgG fall together as the disease is controlled; both are used to track activity.

steps.lead: Niamh stays on **maintenance** immunosuppression with regular **LFTs and IgG** to show the disease is in remission.

steps.title: Managing autoimmune hepatitis
nodes: Confirm: LFTs, antibodies, IgG, biopsy; exclude viral hepatitis
Advanced or refractory disease → liver transplant

steps.lead: If Niamh's disease progressed to decompensated cirrhosis or failed treatment, she would be assessed for a **liver transplant**.
Niamh's plan follows **BSG** and **EASL** guidance on AIH: steroid induction, azathioprine maintenance, TPMT first, and biochemical monitoring.

steps.text: TPMT is checked **before** azathioprine, not after a low count appears. Low TPMT lets the drug accumulate and causes severe **myelosuppression**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why IgG is raised (polyclonal B-cell activation), why TPMT matters (azathioprine metabolism), or how inflammation causes fibrosis (stellate cells).

steps.lead: Niamh's immune system has lost **self-tolerance**: autoreactive T-cells and autoantibodies attack her hepatocytes.

steps.title: From lost tolerance to cirrhosis
nodes: Autoreactive T-cells and autoantibodies target hepatocytes
steps.caption: Treatment aims to stop the chain before the stellate cell step becomes irreversible.

steps.lead: Niamh's ASMA/ANA pattern and organ-specific autoimmunity make her **type 1**; type 2 (anti-LKM) is commoner in children and more aggressive.

steps.q: Why is Niamh's IgG so high?
o: Loss of IgG clearance by the liver
steps.r: The autoimmune drive activates many B-cell clones: a **polyclonal** rise in IgG. A monoclonal band would suggest myeloma.

steps.lead: Niamh's IgG reflects the autoimmune process, and her normal **TPMT** means azathioprine is broken down safely.

visual.title: TPMT activity and azathioprine risk
visual.label: Niamh normal
visual.caption: Low TPMT lets thiopurine metabolites build up in the marrow: pancytopenia.

mcq.q: What is the most important risk factor for autoimmune hepatitis?
Which condition is strongly associated with autoimmune hepatitis?
mcq.r: AIH clusters with **type 1 diabetes**, coeliac, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and thyroid disease.

mcq.q: Which LFT pattern is typical of autoimmune hepatitis?
mcq.r: AIH is **hepatitic**: markedly raised ALT with a normal or mildly raised ALP.

mcq.q: Which antibody is most consistent with type 1 AIH?
mcq.r: **ASMA** (with ANA) is type 1; anti-LKM is type 2.

mcq.q: What is the gold-standard test for autoimmune hepatitis?
mcq.r: **Liver biopsy** is definitive, used alongside the autoantibodies.

mcq.q: Which immunoglobulin is characteristically raised in AIH?
mcq.r: **IgG** is raised in AIH; IgM is the PBC one.

mcq.q: What is the first-line treatment for autoimmune hepatitis?
What must be measured before starting azathioprine?
mcq.r: **TPMT activity**, because low activity risks pancytopenia.

mcq.q: Which cell lays down collagen to cause fibrosis in AIH?
mcq.r: Chronic inflammation activates **hepatic stellate cells**, which deposit collagen.

mcq.q: Which type of AIH is more common in children and more aggressive?
mcq.r: **Type 2** (anti-LKM) affects younger patients and is more aggressive.

technique.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 4 week history of fatigue, poor appetite and aching joints. She has had coeliac disease since childhood. Her sclerae are yellow and the liver edge is palpable 2 cm below the costal margin. She drinks 2 units of alcohol a week and has not travelled. Investigations: ALT 520 IU/L (10–50), ALP 140 IU/L (25–115), IgG 25 g/L (6–16).
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question with deranged LFTs: first decide hepatitic versus cholestatic, then who the patient is.
Young woman with another **autoimmune** disease; arthralgia; ALT-dominant LFTs; raised **IgG**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitic picture + autoimmune background + high IgG = **autoimmune hepatitis**.

elim: 2 units a week is not enough, and AST:ALT would be above 2.
No travel or contacts; high IgG and autoimmune background point away from a virus.
PBC is ALP-dominant with itch, in middle-aged women, and raises IgM.
PSC is ALP-dominant and linked to ulcerative colitis, usually in men.

steps.x: **B. Autoimmune hepatitis.** Rule: young woman + other autoimmunity + ALT-dominant + high IgG = AIH.

technique.stem: A 31 year old woman with vitiligo has jaundice and fatigue. Her ALT is 430 IU/L (10–50), ALP 130 IU/L (25–115) and IgG 22 g/L (6–16). Anti-smooth muscle antibody and ANA are positive. Hepatitis B and C serology are negative. Ultrasound shows a smooth liver with normal bile ducts.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the **diagnostic** test: the one that confirms, not the one that screens.

clues: Anti-smooth muscle antibody and ANA are positive
Hepatitis B and C serology are negative
steps.x: Antibodies already point to type 1 AIH; viral hepatitis excluded; ducts normal so no obstruction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: AIH is confirmed by **liver biopsy** (interface hepatitis), alongside the antibodies.

elim: AMA is for PBC, and the picture is hepatitic.
CT adds nothing once ultrasound is normal.
MRCP looks at bile ducts for PSC; the ducts are normal.
Waiting risks progression to fibrosis; AIH needs diagnosis and treatment.

steps.x: **C. Liver biopsy.** Rule: gold standard for AIH = biopsy; antibodies support but do not confirm.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has biopsy-confirmed autoimmune hepatitis. She was started on prednisolone 6 weeks ago and her ALT has fallen from 600 to 140 IU/L (10–50). Her consultant plans to add a steroid-sparing agent.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: 'Next step' after prednisolone, before a steroid-sparing drug: think about which drug and what it needs first.
She is responding; the steroid-sparing agent in AIH is **azathioprine**, which needs a pre-treatment check.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Measure **TPMT activity** before azathioprine to avoid pancytopenia.

elim: Transplant is for advanced or refractory disease; she is responding.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is for PBC, not AIH.
Stopping steroids abruptly risks a flare and adrenal crisis; they are tapered.
Infliximab is not standard AIH therapy.

steps.x: **A. Check TPMT.** Rule: azathioprine is always preceded by TPMT.

technique.stem: A 26 year old woman with autoimmune thyroid disease has autoimmune hepatitis. Her serum IgG is 30 g/L (6–16). Serum protein electrophoresis shows a diffuse increase in gamma globulins with no paraprotein band.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the raised IgG?
o: Loss of albumin causing compensatory IgG rise

steps.x: A mechanism question: explain one finding (high IgG) in this condition.
A diffuse (not banded) rise means many B-cell clones are involved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The autoimmune process drives **polyclonal B-cell activation**, so IgG rises.

elim: The liver does not clear IgG in a meaningful way.
Hepatocytes make albumin and clotting factors, not immunoglobulins.
Low albumin does not trigger an IgG rise.
A monoclonal process would show a **paraprotein band**, which is absent.

steps.x: **E. Polyclonal B-cell activation.** Rule: diffuse gammopathy = polyclonal = autoimmune drive.

practice.stem: A 22 year old woman has a 3 week history of tiredness, nausea and pain in her wrists. She has type 1 diabetes and pernicious anaemia. She is jaundiced with tender hepatomegaly. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. She drinks no alcohol.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Acute hepatitis-like illness with arthralgia in a young woman with two autoimmune diseases is autoimmune hepatitis. PBC is cholestatic in middle-aged women.

steps.x: Diagnosis: young woman, liver illness, look at her background.
Female, **multiple autoimmune diseases**, arthralgia, acute hepatitis picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune clustering + hepatitis = **AIH**.

elim: Gilbert's gives mild unconjugated jaundice with normal liver and no hepatomegaly or tenderness.
Haemochromatosis presents later, in men, with diabetes from iron, not type 1 at 22.
PBC affects middle-aged women with itch and ALP rise.
Wilson's gives liver plus neuro or psychiatric signs and Kayser-Fleischer rings.

steps.x: **A. Autoimmune hepatitis.** Other autoimmune diseases are the strongest clue after female sex.

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has fatigue and a dull right upper quadrant ache. She has Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Hepatitis B, C and E serology are negative. Ultrasound shows normal bile ducts.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: ALT-dominant LFTs, high IgG and autoimmune thyroid disease with viral causes excluded: autoimmune hepatitis. PBC and PSC are cholestatic.

steps.x: Diagnosis from LFT pattern plus background.
Female with thyroid autoimmunity; viral hepatitis excluded; ducts normal. Labs: ALT-dominant, IgG high.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitic + high IgG + autoimmune background = **AIH**.

elim: No alcohol history and AST:ALT below 1.
NAFLD gives mild ALT rises, not ALT over 400 with high IgG.
PBC is ALP-dominant with raised IgM.
PSC is ALP-dominant with stricturing ducts on imaging.

steps.x: **B. Autoimmune hepatitis.**

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with autoimmune hepatitis is being investigated to classify her disease. She has a sister with type 1 diabetes and she herself has vitiligo. Her ALT is 390 IU/L (10–50) and her ALP is mildly raised.
practice.q: Which is the most likely antibody finding?
practice.e: An adult with personal and family organ-specific autoimmunity has type 1 AIH, defined by ASMA (with ANA). Anti-LKM is type 2, typically children.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: which antibody fits this patient's AIH type.
Adult, organ-specific autoimmunity in her and her family: **type 1** profile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 1 AIH = **ASMA** (and ANA).

elim: Anti-LKM is type 2, more typical of children and young women with aggressive disease.
AMA is PBC.
Anti-tTG is coeliac disease.
p-ANCA is PSC.

steps.x: **C. Anti-smooth muscle antibody.** ASMA is the antibody most consistent with type 1.

practice.stem: A 12 year old girl has a 2 week history of jaundice, abdominal pain and lethargy. Her temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. Her ALT is 890 IU/L (10–50), IgG is raised and ASMA and ANA are negative. Viral serology and caeruloplasmin are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A child with a florid hepatitis, raised IgG, negative ASMA/ANA and negative viral screen fits type 2 AIH (anti-LKM). Normal caeruloplasmin argues against Wilson's.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a child with acute hepatitis and negative 'classic' antibodies.

clues: Viral serology and caeruloplasmin are normal
steps.x: Young female, severe hepatitis, autoimmune marker (IgG) but type 1 antibodies negative; viral and copper causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 2 AIH (**anti-LKM**), which is commoner in children and more aggressive.

elim: Gilbert's never raises ALT.
Viral serology is normal, so hepatitis A IgM would be negative.
PSC is cholestatic and duct-related.
Caeruloplasmin is normal, making Wilson's unlikely.

steps.x: **D. Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.** Negative ASMA/ANA does not exclude AIH: check anti-LKM.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has a 2 month history of fatigue and aching joints, and noticed dark urine last week. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. She has coeliac disease. She is mildly jaundiced.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of these findings?
practice.e: Hepatitic LFTs, high IgG, positive ASMA and negative hepatitis B serology in a woman with coeliac disease: autoimmune hepatitis.

steps.x: A 'most likely cause' of jaundice: classify the LFTs.
Conjugated jaundice (dark urine), arthralgia, coeliac. Labs: ALT-dominant, IgG high, ASMA positive, HBsAg negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatitic + ASMA + IgG = **AIH**.

elim: Gallstone obstruction is ALP-dominant with pain and dilated ducts.
No new drug, and cholestasis is ALP-dominant.
Haemolysis gives unconjugated bilirubin with a normal ALT and no ASMA.
HBsAg is negative.

steps.x: **A. Autoimmune hepatitis.**

practice.stem: A 28 year old woman is referred with an ALT of 350 IU/L (10–50), raised IgG and positive anti-smooth muscle antibody. She feels tired but is otherwise well.
practice.q: Which feature of her history most supports the diagnosis?
practice.e: Autoimmune hepatitis is strongly associated with other autoimmune disease such as type 1 diabetes. Travel and paracetamol point to other causes of hepatitis.

steps.x: A risk factor question: which history item fits AIH.
Labs already say type 1 AIH; the question wants the **associated** feature.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Other autoimmune disease, e.g. **type 1 diabetes**.

elim: Measles has no link with AIH.
Travel suggests hepatitis A or E.
Therapeutic paracetamol does not cause a raised IgG or ASMA.
Smoking is not an AIH risk factor.

steps.x: **E. Type 1 diabetes.** Female sex and other autoimmunity are the risk factors.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has a 3 month history of fatigue. Her ALT is 310 IU/L (10–50), ALP 120 IU/L (25–115) and IgG 20 g/L (6–16). ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody are positive. Hepatitis B and C serology and liver ultrasound are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
practice.e: Liver biopsy is the definitive, gold-standard test for autoimmune hepatitis, interpreted with the autoantibodies.

steps.x: 'Confirm the diagnosis' = gold standard.

clues: ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody are positive
steps.x: Type 1 AIH is likely; viral and structural causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm with **liver biopsy**.

elim: She already has type 1 antibodies; anti-LKM would not confirm.
Fibroscan stages fibrosis but cannot diagnose AIH.
MRCP is for duct disease (PSC).
Caeruloplasmin is for Wilson's; it does not confirm AIH.

steps.x: **C. Liver biopsy.**

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has jaundice and an ALT of 720 IU/L (10–50). Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her IgG is raised and anti-smooth muscle antibody is positive. Autoimmune hepatitis is suspected.
practice.q: Which investigation must be performed before the diagnosis is accepted?
practice.e: Viral hepatitis must be excluded before confirming autoimmune hepatitis, as it gives the same hepatitic picture and steroids could worsen it.

steps.x: 'Must be performed before the diagnosis is accepted': which cause must be excluded.
A hepatitic picture with low-grade fever: an infective hepatitis looks identical.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Exclude **viral hepatitis** with serology before calling it AIH and starting steroids.

elim: AMA is for PBC, which is cholestatic.
CT is not needed; ultrasound images the liver.
Ferritin screens haemochromatosis, unlikely at 25 in a woman.
Thyroid tests are useful but do not exclude a mimic of AIH.

steps.x: **E. Viral hepatitis serology.** Steroids into undiagnosed viral hepatitis is the error to avoid.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has biopsy-confirmed type 1 autoimmune hepatitis. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. She has no ascites or encephalopathy.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: First-line treatment for AIH is immunosuppression with prednisolone. Ursodeoxycholic acid is for PBC; tenofovir and interferon are antivirals.

steps.x: Initial management of confirmed AIH.
Confirmed, compensated AIH with active hepatitis (ALT high, IgG high).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Start **prednisolone**.

elim: Transplant is for advanced or refractory disease; she is compensated.
Ursodeoxycholic acid is PBC treatment.
Interferon can worsen autoimmune disease and is for viral hepatitis.
Tenofovir treats hepatitis B.

steps.x: **B. Oral prednisolone.**

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman with autoimmune hepatitis was started on azathioprine 3 weeks ago without any pre-treatment tests. She now has mouth ulcers and a fever. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 108/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which test would most likely have predicted this complication?
practice.e: Low TPMT activity causes azathioprine accumulation and severe myelosuppression; TPMT must be measured before starting.

steps.x: A management safety question: which pre-treatment test was missed.
Fever and mouth ulcers on azathioprine = **neutropenia / pancytopenia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **TPMT activity** predicts azathioprine marrow toxicity.

elim: Anti-LKM types AIH; it does not predict toxicity.
G6PD predicts haemolysis with oxidant drugs, e.g. primaquine.
HLA-B27 is for spondyloarthropathy.
IgG monitors AIH activity, not drug toxicity.

steps.x: **E. TPMT activity.**

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has had autoimmune hepatitis for 10 years. Despite prednisolone and azathioprine, she now has cirrhosis with ascites, encephalopathy and a bilirubin of 210 μmol/L (<17). Her BP is 98/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Advanced, decompensated or refractory autoimmune hepatitis should be considered for liver transplant.

steps.x: Long-term management of end-stage disease.
Refractory disease with decompensated cirrhosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Liver transplant**.

elim: More azathioprine cannot reverse cirrhosis and risks myelosuppression.
Methotrexate is hepatotoxic and not standard AIH rescue.
Stopping immunosuppression risks a flare.
TIPS treats refractory ascites or varices but worsens encephalopathy and is not a cure.

steps.x: **B. Liver transplant.**

practice.stem: A 29 year old woman has a liver biopsy for autoimmune hepatitis. It shows interface hepatitis and bands of collagen linking portal tracts. Her ALT has been raised for over 2 years.
practice.q: Which cell is most likely responsible for the collagen deposition?
practice.e: Chronic immune-mediated inflammation activates hepatic stellate cells, which deposit collagen and cause fibrosis and cirrhosis.

steps.x: A mechanism question: which cell makes the scar.
Chronic inflammation has led to **fibrosis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Activated **hepatic stellate cells** lay down collagen.

elim: Cholangiocytes line bile ducts; they do not make the fibrous bands.
Hepatocytes are the target of injury, not the collagen source.
Kupffer cells release signals that activate stellate cells but do not lay down collagen.
Plasma cells make antibodies (IgG) in the infiltrate.

steps.x: **B. Hepatic stellate cell.**

prompts.q: What is autoimmune hepatitis and what does it lead to if untreated?

points.why: It can present acutely but is a chronic disease.
Hepatocyte (not bile duct) injury gives the hepatitic LFTs.

points.p: Leads to fibrosis and cirrhosis if untreated

prompts.q: Who gets autoimmune hepatitis? Name the risk factors and associated conditions.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem gives you a young woman with another autoimmune disease.

points.why: A personal history is the second big clue.
Any of these in a stem with hepatitis = think AIH.
First-degree relatives may have Graves' or type 1 diabetes.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: an acute-hepatitis-like illness, or nothing at all.

points.why: Many are picked up on routine bloods.
A clue pointing to autoimmune rather than viral.

points.p: Hepatomegaly or signs of chronic liver disease

prompts.q: Which features distinguish type 1 from type 2 autoimmune hepatitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: antibody and age decide the type.

points.p: Type 1: ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody
points.why: ASMA is most consistent with type 1.

points.p: Type 2: children and young women, more aggressive
points.why: Think type 2 if the stem is a child.

prompts.q: How do you tell AIH from PBC and PSC on bloods?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: LFT pattern, antibody and immunoglobulin.

points.p: AIH: ALT-dominant, ALP normal or mildly raised

points.why: Often a young man with UC.

prompts.q: What are the first-line investigations in suspected autoimmune hepatitis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: LFTs, antibodies, IgG, exclude viruses, image.

points.why: Markedly raised ALT, mildly raised ALP.

points.p: Viral hepatitis serology to exclude infection

prompts.q: What is the gold-standard test for autoimmune hepatitis?

points.why: Shows interface hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate.

prompts.q: How is autoimmune hepatitis treated, from first-line to refractory disease?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: steroid, then steroid-sparer, then transplant.

points.p: Maintenance immunosuppression, monitor LFTs and IgG
Advanced or refractory disease: liver transplant
points.why: For decompensated cirrhosis or treatment failure.

prompts.q: Why does autoimmune hepatitis cause cirrhosis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tolerance lost, hepatocytes attacked, stellate cells make collagen.

points.p: Autoreactive T-cells and autoantibodies target hepatocyte antigens
points.why: ANA, ASMA and anti-LKM are the markers.

points.p: Collagen deposition causes fibrosis then cirrhosis

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one immune mechanism, one drug metabolism mechanism.

glossary.AIH: Autoimmune hepatitis: chronic immune attack on liver cells.
glossary.ALT: Alanine aminotransferase, a liver enzyme released when hepatocytes are damaged.
glossary.AST: Aspartate aminotransferase, a liver (and muscle) enzyme released by cell damage.
glossary.ALP: Alkaline phosphatase, an enzyme raised mainly in bile duct obstruction (cholestasis).
glossary.GGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase, a liver enzyme raised in cholestasis and alcohol use.
glossary.hepatitic: An LFT pattern where transaminases (ALT/AST) rise far more than ALP, meaning liver cell injury.
glossary.cholestatic: An LFT pattern where ALP and GGT rise most, meaning impaired bile flow.
glossary.ASMA: Anti-smooth muscle antibody, the autoantibody most consistent with type 1 autoimmune hepatitis.
glossary.ANA: Antinuclear antibody, an autoantibody against cell nuclei; positive in type 1 AIH and lupus.
glossary.anti-LKM: Anti-liver/kidney microsomal antibody, the marker of type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.
glossary.AMA: Anti-mitochondrial antibody, the marker of primary biliary cholangitis.
glossary.p-ANCA: Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis.
glossary.IgG: Immunoglobulin G, the main antibody class; markedly raised in autoimmune hepatitis.
glossary.IgM: Immunoglobulin M; characteristically raised in primary biliary cholangitis.
glossary.TPMT: Thiopurine methyltransferase, the enzyme that breaks down azathioprine; low activity causes marrow toxicity.
glossary.azathioprine: A thiopurine immunosuppressant used as a steroid-sparing drug.
glossary.prednisolone: An oral corticosteroid used to suppress inflammation and the immune system.
glossary.steroid-sparing: A drug added so that the steroid dose can be reduced or stopped.
glossary.pancytopenia: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together.
glossary.myelosuppression: Reduced bone marrow production of blood cells.
glossary.interface hepatitis: Biopsy finding where inflammation spills from portal tracts into surrounding liver cells; typical of AIH.
glossary.hepatic stellate cells: Liver cells that, when activated by inflammation, produce collagen and cause fibrosis.
glossary.fibrosis: Scar tissue laid down after repeated injury.
glossary.cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver with regenerative nodules and loss of function.
glossary.self-tolerance: The immune system's normal ability not to attack the body's own tissues.
glossary.polyclonal: Coming from many different B-cell clones, giving a diffuse rise in antibodies.
glossary.paraprotein: A single monoclonal antibody band on electrophoresis, as in myeloma.
glossary.PBC: Primary biliary cholangitis: autoimmune destruction of small bile ducts; AMA positive.
glossary.PSC: Primary sclerosing cholangitis: stricturing of bile ducts, linked to ulcerative colitis.
glossary.MRCP: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, an MRI scan of the bile ducts.
glossary.ursodeoxycholic acid: A bile acid used to treat primary biliary cholangitis.
glossary.vitiligo: Autoimmune loss of skin pigment, giving white patches.
glossary.pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor causing vitamin B12 deficiency.
glossary.coeliac disease: Immune reaction to gluten that damages the small bowel lining.
glossary.Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid causing hypothyroidism.
glossary.EASL: European Association for the Study of the Liver.
glossary.INR: International normalised ratio, a clotting test that reflects liver synthetic function.
glossary.Kupffer cell: Resident macrophage of the liver sinusoids.
